Tuesday 24 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Andy Burnham tells MPs it would be unthinkable to rejoin the European Union without a referendum as Louise Haigh reviews abolishing Natural England and the Environment Agency and Tata’s Somerset gigafactory loses its second contractor.
  • NATO chief Mark Rutte vows to defend against space threats after reports of a Russian nuclear-armed satellite while leaked death certificates reveal 460,000 Russian war fatalities and more than 1,000 military suicides.
  • Brazil’s Centrão parties back Lula’s fiscal package in the Chamber of Deputies in pursuit of ministries and unlocked amendments as a Federal Police report on Alexandre de Moraes omits 47 messages with Daniel Vorcaro.
  • Nvidia unanimously reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive after direct intervention from Donald Trump, sparking a $1 trillion stock market rally while Australia agrees 5 per cent global revenue fines for big tech platforms.
  • The £437 million revamped London Museum is unveiled inside Smithfield Market as Steven Spielberg and Paul Thomas Anderson team up for a western and Grand Theft Auto VI sets PlayStation’s all-time launch record.
  • FIFA confirms the United Kingdom as host of the 2035 Women’s World Cup as leaked files expose Gianni Infantino’s scrapped 96-year World Cup sell-off plan and Brentford rout 10-man Everton 4–0.

News

Burnham calls rejoining EU without a referendum unthinkable as Haigh weighs scrapping nature watchdogs and Somerset gigafactory loses second builder

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the House of Commons on Monday that rejoining the European Union without another referendum would be “unthinkable”, offering his clearest commitment yet to a public vote if he eventually concludes Britain should return to the bloc. Updating MPs on Friday’s Brussels summit—which covered food and drink border checks, emissions trading, and youth mobility, and will be enacted through Thursday’s European Partnerships Bill—Burnham dismissed warnings from former Tory premiers David Cameron, Theresa May, and Rishi Sunak against reopening Brexit, calling them “stuck in the past” over a bad deal. While declining to rule out a referendum pledge at the next election, Burnham promised “no banging on about Europe” and said No 10 had “no fixed destination” as it watches upcoming elections in EU states such as France. Rival campaigns Stay Out and the European Movement-backed Get In have already launched, while Whitehall officials questioned whether Burnham’s 120-strong “Number 10 North” office in Manchester has the clout to deliver next month’s 10-year reindustrialisation plan and his New Year “rewiring the state” white paper. (Guardian, BBC, BBC)

That state-rewiring drive drew immediate criticism from green groups after de facto Deputy Prime Minister Louise Haigh told the CBI conference that Natural England, the Environment Agency, Ofwat, and the Drinking Water Inspectorate are under review for possible abolition to curb more than 20 statutory planning consultees. In an open letter, the RSPB, the Wildlife Trusts, the National Trust, and the British Trust for Ornithology warned that scrapping the only regulator with a legal duty to protect nature would leave Britain exposed to floods, fires, droughts, and extinctions despite government impact assessments finding minimal evidence that environmental rules block housebuilding. Meanwhile, Green Party leader Zack Polanski backed a Verdant thinktank report by Sacha Deshmukh endorsing UK membership of NATO, off-the-shelf procurement, and nuclear weapons maintenance cooperation with France—breaking with the party’s 2024 pledge to dismantle Trident immediately after YouGov polling showed only 17 per cent of voters trust the Greens on defence. (Guardian, Guardian)

Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms’s final Personal Independence Payment (PIP) review, published on Tuesday afternoon, recommends linking awards for England and Wales’s four million claimants to real-life extra costs rather than diagnoses and fast-tracking the most severely disabled 10 per cent without reassessment, while proposing no major cuts despite annual PIP spending rising from £16.3 billion pre-pandemic to £32.1 billion now and a projected £41.5 billion by 2030–31. In Somerset, Tata-owned battery maker Agratas lost its second lead builder in five months on its £5.2 billion Bridgwater gigafactory for Jaguar Land Rover—backed by £380 million in state aid—after contractor TSL walked away over cost and timeline disputes following June’s sacking of Sir Robert McAlpine, clouding its January 2028 target. Simultaneously, European benchmark Dutch month-ahead gas prices jumped up to 8.6 per cent to €96.08 per megawatt-hour on Monday amid a forecast cold snap, Qatari supply slowdowns, and continental storage at 69 per cent against an 80 per cent norm, prompting Citizens Advice chief Clare Moriarty to warn that Chancellor John Healey’s £100 council-tax rebate will be swallowed by Ofgem’s expected 26 per cent (£443) January price cap rise. (BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

In housing, Hamptons forecast that British rents will rise 14.2 per cent between 2026 and 2029—nearly double the 7.2 per cent house-price forecast—after rental supply fell 26 per cent nationwide and 39 per cent in London over a decade, making buying cheaper than renting in seven of 12 major cities outside London led by Glasgow (£288 a month cheaper) as Savills projected record corporate build-to-rent investment following May’s Renters’ Rights Act. Elsewhere, Education Secretary Lucy Powell took 18 university leaders to Beijing for the first UK–China education summit in nine years to defend a £7 billion sector serving 150,000 Chinese students, two months after MI5 warned that a Chinese front body had covertly funded over 100 UK academics; cross-party MPs urged Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to mandate public company registers in the British Virgin Islands, Cayman Islands, and Turks and Caicos; Bristol signed a three-year reparative twinning pact with Speightstown, Barbados; and the High Court heard that Turkish heiress Nebahat Isbilen paid Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor £750,000 in 2019—later repaid, with Andrew summoned for 14 December—after adviser Selman Turk allegedly claimed it was needed for passport help, alongside £210,000 routed to Sarah Ferguson. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

NATO vows space defence over Russian nuclear satellite reports as leaked files expose 460,000 Russian war deaths and over 1,000 suicides

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte pledged in Berlin on Monday that the alliance would defend every inch of its territory, including in space, after German broadcasters NDR and WDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung reported intelligence shared among NATO allies warning that Russia could launch a nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon dubbed “Sputnik-S” within 60 days. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the reports showed the escalation Moscow is prepared to pursue in breach of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, while European Space Agency chief Josef Aschbacher called orbital nuclear weapons “the ultimate nightmare scenario” and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the reports as propaganda. The alert followed a brief Russian drone incursion into Polish airspace during overnight strikes on western Ukraine, days after Russian projectiles landed 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise in Poland. Meanwhile, Libya’s UN-backed government in Tripoli demanded an explanation from Kyiv after Ukraine’s SBU confirmed that seven mothership-launched sea drones sank the Russian Navy corvette Merkury and hit a weapons cargo vessel in Khalifa Haftar-held Benghazi. (BBC, Guardian, BBC)

Inside Russia’s military, an analysis of more than 11 million confidential Rosstat death certificates obtained by Belarusian opposition hackers Cyber Partisans and Ukrainian collective Silent Crow identified over 460,000 Russian war deaths between February 2022 and September 2026, making war the leading cause of death for Russian men under 65 last year. The files record at least 1,087 military suicides—614 in occupied Ukraine or border regions such as Belgorod and Bryansk, including 29-year-old Sergeant Alexei Bolgov near Donetsk—alongside 885 firearm deaths of “undetermined intent” that frequently mask suicides, together equating to an entire regiment amid widespread coercion, physical abuse, and open-ended contracts. (Guardian, Guardian)

Following Sunday’s collapse of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, former US vice-president Al Gore, Potsdam Institute director Johan Rockström, and Australian negotiations president Chris Bowen urged an overhaul of the UN consensus rule after petrostates blocked a fossil-fuel phaseout and stalled a goal to lift electricity’s share of global energy use from 20 to 35 per cent by 2035 amid surging AI data-centre demand. In his opening 2026 BBC Radio 4 Reith Lecture, Cambridge professor Robert Macfarlane called trust in COP summits misplaced, backing smaller fossil-fuel phaseout alliances such as the Santa Marta process while condemning the “end-times tech bro” and Mars colonisation. (Guardian, The Verge, Guardian)

In the US, a Second Circuit appeals panel reversed the late Judge Alvin Hellerstein’s refusal to move Donald Trump’s New York hush-money conviction to federal court, pausing his state appeal and offering a route to seek dismissal of his 34 felony counts on presidential immunity grounds. Elsewhere, Israeli academics and rights groups Standing Together and Ir Amim demanded the release of 26-year-old Hebrew University student Mahdi Tounsi, who appeared on video link bruised, without his glasses, and with his hair and beard shaved after his 8 November dorm arrest and an administrative detention order signed by Defence Minister Israel Katz; French campaigner Gisèle Pelicot announced legal action against publisher Tinbad and author Sabine Prokhoris for sending journalists non-consensual nude photos taken by her convicted ex-husband to promote a book; China announced a death sentence for an official surnamed Ma over leaking 35 state secrets for $150,000; and Iran flogged a singer and four others for performing without a hijab. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Centrão backs Lula’s fiscal package in pursuit of ministries as PF report on Moraes omits 47 Vorcaro messages and STF vacancy tops 400 days

Centrão parties delivered 83 per cent of their votes—211 of 254 deputies—in an extraordinary Monday night session of Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies convened by Speaker Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB) to approve the base text of Planning Minister Bruno Moretti’s fiscal adjustment package. Motivated by currency jitters after the real touched R$ 6 to the dollar on Monday and by talks over President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s fourth-term cabinet and nearly R$ 3 billion in blocked parliamentary amendments, União Brasil gave 44 of 50 votes as Pedro Lucas Fernandes and Moses Rodrigues bid to retain the Regional Integration and Tourism ministries, while Republicanos gave 36 of 42 votes as it seeks a second ministry and Caixa Econômica Federal. Earlier, the Finance Ministry cut its GDP growth forecast to 1.9 per cent for 2026 and 1.8 per cent for 2027—below the 2.4 per cent budget projection—and raised IPCA inflation estimates to 5.3 per cent this year and 4.5 per cent next year, while Senate President Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil-AP) courted first-term senators ahead of February’s leadership vote against Rogério Marinho (PL-RN) and Tereza Cristina (PP-MS) by promising faster release of non-mandatory committee amendments. (Folha, Meio, Folha, Folha)

At the Supreme Federal Court (STF), disclosures showed that the report sent by Federal Police chief Andrei Rodrigues to STF President Edson Fachin on Justice Alexandre de Moraes’s ties to arrested Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro relied solely on keyword searches, omitting 47 screenshots of notes-app messages exchanged in late 2025 as well as two Banco Master contracts with the law firm of Moraes’s wife, Viviane Barci de Moraes: a R$ 131 million retainer and a R$ 50 million share transfer in a Legacy jet and helicopter. In the omitted messages before his Guarulhos Airport arrest over fraudulent credit sales to BRB, Vorcaro asked whether Central Bank chief Gabriel Galípolo knew and whether Prosecutor-General Paulo Gonet or Rodrigues could reverse the probe. Meanwhile, the STF vacancy left by Justice Luís Roberto Barroso’s October 2025 retirement passed 400 days—the longest since 1985, four times the 100-day average—leaving 64 cases suspended by tie votes after the Senate rejected Lula’s nominee Jorge Messias in April. (Folha, Folha)

On the right, former president Jair Bolsonaro—hospitalised from house arrest with a small-intestine blockage—was diagnosed with bilateral aspiration pneumonia at Brasília’s DF Star ICU, where doctors Brasil Caiado and Claudio Birolini kept him on antibiotics and a nasogastric tube. The stay sparked a public clash between his son Carlos Bolsonaro, who noted on X that no family member was present while Michelle Bolsonaro returned from Israel, and the former first lady, who rebuked pessimistic posts before Carlos shared a photo of his father’s feeding tube. With Flávio and Eduardo Bolsonaro in the US and Nikolas Ferreira clashing with PL chief Valdemar Costa Neto, São Paulo Governor Tarcísio de Freitas positioned himself for 2030 by retaining 11 of 18 state secretaries and concentrating budget and regulatory power under former federal aides Natália Resende and Rafael Benini, while the Federal Police opened an R$ 11.4 million tender for three rifle-resistant presidential sedans for Lula without sunroofs, citing Benazir Bhutto’s 2007 assassination. (Folha, Folha, Meio, Folha, Folha)

Technology

Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang after Trump intervenes to spark $1 trillion rally as Australia agrees 5 per cent global revenue fines for big tech

Six days after Nvidia chair Harvey Jones declared that the board would not reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang following his 12 November resignation over relationships with two subordinates and an admitted affair with suspected Chinese intelligence intermediary Alice Huang—former head of Singapore’s Megaspeed, suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China—directors voted unanimously on Sunday night to restore him as CEO, president, and director, replacing interim chief Colette Kress. President Donald Trump had sent Vice-President JD Vance to reassure the board on national security and dialled into Sunday’s meeting to overrule Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s call for an outside hire, boasting on CNBC that “I made the deal” and posting an AI image on Truth Social of Huang’s face on Trump’s bloodied body raising a red bra. Cheering staff greeted Huang at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters on Monday as shares surged 32 per cent to add over $1 trillion in value, lifting Nvidia back above $4 trillion after an AI tech rout had dragged the Nasdaq 5 per cent below its 1 January level despite Anthropic’s stock debut, while House Democrats vowed to investigate Trump and Huang when the CEO testifies next week. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, The Verge, The Verge, Guardian)

In Australia, Communications Minister Anika Wells agreed amendments with the Greens on Tuesday to pass Digital Duty of Care laws this week, exposing platforms and chatbots to fines of up to A$109 million or 5 per cent of global revenue, creating a private right for citizens to sue big tech for online harm, and letting users opt out of addictive algorithms and endless scrolling from late 2027. Meanwhile, over 150 child safety groups including Jonathan Haidt’s Anxious Generation Movement and 52 UK parliamentarians urged Amazon, eBay, and Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds to halt Christmas sales of nearly 80 AI toys after tests found a ChatGPT-linked plush bunny for three-year-olds discussing sexual consent, while aviation analyst Bob Mann Jr attributed mid-November’s US FAA flight grounding to the rollout of its AI-assisted Smart System rather than an Arkansas router. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

As autonomous agents advance, JPMorgan Chase banned third-party AI agents logging in with customer credentials and Bank of America, Citibank, PNC, and Wells Fargo warned users that agent use is at their own risk ahead of Apple’s expected agentic Siri in iOS 28. For developers, Anthropic launched Claude Ship in beta (`/ship`), pairing Code Review, PR Steward, and Claude Approvals agents to review, fix, and merge GitHub pull requests alongside a revamped mobile app, while OpenAI brought GPT-6.2 Sol to ChatGPT’s main tab and set a 23 December retirement for GPT-5.6 Sol and Terra. On the open web, Andreas Kling released the first macOS and Linux alpha of the independent Rust-ported Ladybird browser engine; Kagi launched its ad-free $99-a-year Kagi Mail beta; and a coalition of 55,000 EU businesses including Mozilla, Vivaldi, and Shopify petitioned Ursula von der Leyen over Apple’s rules forcing non-WebKit browsers into separate EU-only apps. (9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, The Verge, The Verge, MacMagazine)

In Apple hardware and software, reviews of the £1,999 foldable iPhone Duo praised its matt 7.6-inch internal OLED screen, 5.4-inch outer display, and right-edge iOS dock while noting its squat 84.1-millimetre width requires two hands and its soft inner screen dents under a fingernail. Apple also advertised four silicon photonics engineering roles for optical data-centre interconnects amid M8 Ultra server rumours; completed its US Apple Pay rollout at Walmart and Sam’s Club alongside iOS 27’s card grid, Amex point redemptions, and Tap to Share; named its 2026 App Store Award finalists including Ulysses, Things, and Big Walk; prepared (PRODUCT)RED editions of HomePod mini 2 and AirPods Max 2 for 1 December and a 3 December reopening of its Reading store at The Oracle after closing Basingstoke; and saw Meta launch Edits for iPadOS as open-source tool HomePod Hospital enabled Linux on first-generation HomePods. (Guardian, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, MacStories, MacMagazine, MacMagazine, MacMagazine, MacMagazine)

Culture

New £437m London Museum shines at Smithfield as Spielberg and Paul Thomas Anderson team up for a western and GTA VI breaks PlayStation records

After a 10-year, £437 million overhaul of Smithfield’s 1883 Victorian General Market, the rebranded London Museum—formerly isolated on its 1976 London Wall roundabout—has unveiled its cathedral-like home beneath the rooftop sign “All the grit and the glitters”. Designed by Stanton Williams, Asif Khan, and Julian Harrap Architects under Horace Jones’s glazed dome and brick vaults, it turns 44 former butcher units into 250 metres of street frontages while displaying Tudor jewels, Syd’s century-old coffee stall, and a preserved piece of the Whitechapel fatberg. In Illinois, artist Theaster Gates bought Antioch’s 60,000-square-foot Pickard China factory—America’s last fine porcelain maker, where 12 staff still produce White House tableware beneath tarpaulin-patched roofs. (Guardian, Guardian)

In film and television, Steven Spielberg announced he will direct an adaptation of Kevin Barry’s 1890s western novel The Heart in Winter from a script by Paul Thomas Anderson—Anderson’s first full screenplay for another director—starring Oscar winners Jessie Buckley, Cillian Murphy, and Mark Rylance for release in 2028. At the box office, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s $7 million A24 Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything passed $102.5 million globally after a UK record £2.4 million opening for a non-music documentary. Meanwhile, John Hamburg’s fourth comedy outing Focker In-Law drew two-star reviews despite adding Ariana Grande alongside Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro, and Apple TV renewed Ted Lasso for a fifth season while ordering a Timberlake docuseries and expanding James Marsden’s CIA thriller Disavowed. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, The Verge, MacMagazine, MacMagazine)

Following Grand Theft Auto VI’s $3.79 billion opening day, Sony confirmed it was the largest launch in PlayStation history, with 39 million unique PS5 players logging 683 million hours (17.4 hours each) and driving the biggest non-holiday spike in new PS5 console activations since 2020. Comcast recorded its highest-ever internet traffic day (24 per cent of peak traffic), while Alinea Analytics reported a 42 per cent drop in Call of Duty’s daily players from 7.6 million to 4.4 million. In London, 2022 GTA VI leaker Arion Kurtaj received a seven-year sentence but was released on licence for time served under a five-year Discord and Telegram ban. Inside Leonida, Luther Archer confirmed that his late brother D’Angelo recorded the newly uncovered funk track Kamikaze in November 2024 with Slingbaum, Yussef Dayes, and James Gadson before dying in October 2025, while YouTuber Memeio followed power lines across 12 substations to enter the Vice City cheat code “Life is passing me by”, opening a portal to a polygonal 1980s Malibu Club featuring Danny Dyer as Kent Paul. (IGN, IGN, The Verge, IGN, IGN)

Sports

FIFA confirms UK as 2035 Women’s World Cup host as leaked files expose Infantino’s 96-year sell-off plan, Raya avoids surgery and Brentford rout Everton

A special virtual FIFA Congress ratified England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland on Monday as co-hosts of the 48-team, 104-match 2035 Women’s World Cup—Britain’s first World Cup since 1966, using at least 19 stadiums across the four nations alongside a UK push to bring one million more girls into football and counter online manosphere misogyny—while approving the US, Mexico, Costa Rica, and Jamaica for 2031. Hours earlier, leaked internal FIFA memos from 17 and 18 July with Thrive Capital (“Project Box”) revealed that Gianni Infantino’s scrapped $20 billion FIFA Forward Enterprise plan would have transferred commercial rights for FIFA events to a for-profit subsidiary over rolling 12-year licences for up to 96 years without a tender, backed by a $250 million break fee and a 5 per cent management bonus pool worth $50 million per $1 billion added above $20 billion. (BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

In the Premier League on Monday night, Brentford climbed to sixth by routing 10-man Everton 4–0, spoiling David Moyes’s club-record 593rd match in charge. Converted left-back Keane Lewis-Potter scored twice via deflections before Everton captain James Tarkowski received his first red card in 351 Premier League games (after a record 74 bookings) following a VAR review for a studs-up challenge on Yehor Yarmoliuk, ruling him out of Sunday’s Merseyside derby before Vitaly Janelt’s long-range strike and Fábio Carvalho’s late fourth completed the win. Meanwhile, pundits debated the “Grand Theft Auto effect” after Manchester United’s Bryan Mbeumo posted a past-midnight GTA VI photo before Sunday’s 4–0 loss at Liverpool, where United conceded 28 shots ahead of Wednesday’s Champions League trip to Sporting. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

Ahead of Tuesday’s Champions League fixtures, Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta confirmed that goalkeeper David Raya needs no surgery on the shoulder injured at Newcastle and could return against Manchester City on Sunday, with Kepa Arrizabalaga deputising against Niko Kovač’s Borussia Dortmund and Jobe Bellingham. Aston Villa manager Unai Emery kept Monday training at Bodymoor Heath after UEFA barred Villa from practising on Galatasaray’s sandy, emergency-repaired Rams Park surface in Istanbul, while Paris Saint-Germain lost forward Désiré Doué for the season to a right ACL tear sustained six minutes after scoring at Nice, joining winger Khvicha Kvaratskhelia on the sidelines. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Monday 23 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • COP31 climate talks collapse without a central agreement in Antalya after the EU, the UK, and developing nations reject a text omitting fossil fuels, while suspected Ukrainian sea drones sink a Russian corvette in Libya.
  • Thirty-one NHS hospital trusts warn that budget-cutting demands threaten patient care as Sir Stephen Timms calls for a fundamental overhaul of PIP assessments and Andy Burnham defends his EU deal in Parliament.
  • Federal Police files sharpen an internal Supreme Court dispute over who oversees Brazil’s Banco Master inquiry as lawmakers advance plans to pave 400 kilometres of the BR-319 highway through the Amazon in 2027.
  • US intelligence chief Jay Clayton and Microsoft President Brad Smith warn of months of further tech outages after a Delta hub failure in Atlanta, while AI video reskinning and Black Friday clone storefronts spread online.
  • Late novelist Dame Jilly Cooper is accused of extensive plagiarism in her 1978 romance Prudence as Rockstar Games explains why darts and bowling were cut from Grand Theft Auto VI and Nan Goldin opens at the Hayward Gallery.
  • Liverpool rout 10-man Manchester United 4–0 at Anfield to inflict the joint-heaviest debut defeat in the club’s history on Mauricio Pochettino, while Hull City stun Brighton and FIFA prepares to confirm the UK as 2035 Women’s World Cup host.

News

COP31 climate summit collapses without a deal in Antalya as Ukrainian sea drones sink Russian warship in Libya and strikes kill 13 near Kyiv

United Nations climate talks at the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, broke down on Sunday afternoon after running more than 40 hours past their Friday deadline, becoming the longest UN climate conference on record and the first since Copenhagen in 2009 to fail to adopt a central political deal. Turkish COP President Murat Kurum and Australian negotiations president Chris Bowen abandoned their proposed “Antalya pact” cover decision after nearly 40 nations registered objections on the plenary floor. While a Saudi-led bloc refused any text endorsing a transition away from fossil fuels, a coalition of over 130 countries—led by the European Union, the UK, Norway, Panama, the Marshall Islands, and least-developed states—rejected a diluted text that omitted the words “fossil fuels”, promoted carbon capture, and spoke only of an “irreversible transition towards lower greenhouse gas emissions”. Speaking for the EU to applause, Irish Environment Minister Darragh O’Brien said the text failed to respond to science and that Brussels would never endorse greenwashing. (Guardian, BBC)

At his final COP before stepping down as UN Secretary-General, António Guterres expressed deep disappointment and accused fossil-fuel interests of copying Big Tobacco’s playbook by distorting science and blocking policy while piling up profits. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese cited difficult geopolitical times, whereas Climate Analytics chief Bill Hare praised governments for rejecting a hollow text and argued Australia should never again co-chair talks while exporting fossil fuels. Simultaneously, campaigners condemned wealthy nations for blocking adaptation finance: Climate Action Network director Tasneem Essop called Antalya the worst COP ever, and Power Shift Africa’s Mohamed Adow faulted Europe for demanding fossil-fuel roadmaps while withholding funds and expanding domestic oil and gas. Delegates passed only minor side measures, including a just-transition mechanism that Indigenous leader Edson Krenak and former Colombian minister Irene Vélez Torres called inadequate. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

Russia’s war against Ukraine expanded into the central Mediterranean at dawn on Sunday when suspected Ukrainian sea drones struck and sank the Merkury, a Russian Navy Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette refuelling at Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya, over 1,000 miles from southern Ukraine. Authorities aligned with General Khalifa Haftar said four sea drones were intercepted before two hit the warship, with Planet Labs and Vantor satellite imagery showing the vessel capsized and sunk; hours later, another sea drone struck the Russia-linked cargo ship Ascalon off Benghazi, prompting the UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL) to warn against Libya becoming a foreign battleground. In Ukraine’s Kyiv region, rescuers in Dymer dug for 14 hours on Sunday to pull a seven-year-old boy and a 79-year-old woman alive from a bombed residential building where overnight Russian strikes killed nine people, while separate attacks killed one person in Bila Tserkva and three at a grocery store in Vyshneve. (Guardian, BBC, BBC)

In the Middle East, an Oxfam and Conflict and Environment Observatory report found that Israel’s campaign in Gaza—which has killed over 74,000 Palestinians and wounded 175,000—has left a “toxic wasteland” of heavy metals, asbestos, munitions residue, and raw sewage that Oxfam chief Amitabh Behar termed environmental war crimes. In the West Bank, Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot—tasked with forming a government after October’s inconclusive election denied Benjamin Netanyahu a majority—condemned settler arson attacks on four Palestinian villages including Kafr Malik as “Jewish terrorism” stoked by ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. In the US, Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated 21-year Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx by 330 votes after a North Carolina recount, giving Democrats at least 258 House seats to Republicans’ 173—the largest majority since 1992—and vowing to probe Donald Trump’s business conflicts as Trump hosted his third $TRUMP meme-coin gala in Virginia, where over half of leaderboard wallets linked to foreign exchanges. Meanwhile, Seattle-Tacoma airport saw protests after masked ICE agents detained father Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and daughter Sofia Hernandez Mejia on an Alaska Airlines jet bridge, and the US Army invoked emergency rules to bypass a court stay and detonate unstable explosives in Middletown, Iowa. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Thirty-one NHS trusts warn of unpalatable cuts as Timms calls for PIP overhaul and Burnham defends EU reset before MPs

Thirty-one NHS hospital trusts in England have warned in their risk registers that NHS England savings demands threaten patient care and normal operations. Twenty-seven cited lack of money as their top threat, and six—London’s King’s College Hospital (£85 million savings target) and St George’s, Epsom and St Helier (£91 million), plus North Midlands, Gloucestershire, Doncaster and Bassetlaw, and Birmingham and Solihull mental health trusts—gave finances the maximum risk score of 25 as trusts seek up to £106 million each amid drug inflation, strikes, heatwaves, and IT rollouts. East Kent cancer patients waited up to a month for pre-chemotherapy appointments after bank-nurse pay cuts; York and Scarborough shut a 28-bed Bridlington step-down ward and weighed cutting urgent treatment hours; Harrogate ended 15 years of rural out-of-hours GP cover; and Sherwood Forest moved to close King’s Mill Hospital’s hydrotherapy pool. To ease clinical workloads, the NHS launched the EDITH trial across 30 sites starting at Cambridge University Hospitals, inviting 700,000 women aged 50 to 71 to test artificial intelligence replacing one of two human mammogram readers. (Guardian, BBC)

Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms confirmed that his review of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), due on Tuesday, will recommend a “fundamental overhaul” of assessments while keeping the benefit for all adult ages. Co-chaired with disability advocates Clenton Farquharson and Sharon Brennan, the review deems the 13-year-old setup unfit for purpose amid rising mental health and neurodivergent claims and proposes a fast track for lifelong, degenerative, or terminal conditions. Retaining universal eligibility contrasts with Alan Milburn’s NEETs report last week, which proposed scrapping PIP for under-25s to save £3.6 billion, handing Prime Minister Andy Burnham a delicate choice after 120 Labour MPs rebelled against £5 billion in welfare cuts in 2025. On Monday, Burnham will tell MPs that Friday’s Brussels deal—ending most food, plant, and animal border checks from 1 March 2028 alongside carbon-market and youth-mobility pacts—is this parliament’s biggest growth measure, worth 0.5 per cent of GDP (£17 billion). While Scottish seed potato exporter Jamieson Brothers welcomed reopening a £112 million trade, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch will tell the CBI that Burnham botched the talks even as polling shows 512 of 632 British seats favour rejoining the EU and Theresa May urged politicians on BBC One to move on from Brexit. (Guardian, BBC, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

Burnham also faces a winter squeeze ahead of Wednesday’s Ofgem decision, with Cornwall Insight forecasting a 26 per cent (£443) rise in January’s typical annual energy price cap to £2,166 as Middle East turmoil and 3.6 per cent inflation hit northern towns hardest. Centrica chief Chris O’Shea warned that £5 billion in household energy arrears will climb as non-payment adds £1.60 a week to paying customers’ bills, while Poundland—with 600 stores and 11,000 staff—has days to find a buyer after owner Gordon Brothers froze £50 million despite an £18.1 million profit turnaround. Elsewhere, TaxWatch FOI data showed UK taxpayers’ offshore tax-haven funds topped £1 trillion after a 10 per cent rise as HMRC assigned compliance managers to 200 billionaires; police evacuated 12,000 fans from Manchester’s Co-op Live after a suspected tear-gas release at Don Toliver’s concert left 50 treated; RAF chief Sir Harv Smyth said the 2035 Tempest jet could be Britain’s last crewed fighter as autonomous jets fly next year; a probe found police and medics twice released paranoid schizophrenic Alexander Lewis-Ranwell before he killed three Exeter men in their 80s; Laura Brand vowed on YouTube to obey prison rules; and historians showed four 19th-century Bank of England directors profited from post-abolition Cuban slavery. (BBC, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, BBC, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Federal Police reports deepen Brazil’s Supreme Court rift over Banco Master as Amazon highway BR-319 paving advances for 2027

The transfer of four Federal Police (PF) reports mentioning Supreme Federal Court (STF) justices to Prosecutor-General Paulo Gonet has opened an internal clash over who will oversee the Banco Master investigation. The inquiry into former banker Daniel Vorcaro’s ties to senior magistrates is on its third rapporteur since November 2025: after Justice Dias Toffoli recused himself and Justice André Mendonça ran the case from February to 12 September, STF President Edson Fachin temporarily took control. Mendonça’s allies view the decision by Fachin and PF director-general Andrei Rodrigues—whom Mendonça had previously ordered removed—to send a report citing Mendonça to the Prosecutor-General’s Office rather than archiving it alongside six other thin files as a move to oust him and stall operations. Conversely, justices close to Alexandre de Moraes argue Mendonça’s selective disclosures and personal ties make his position untenable, urging that the case move from the Second Panel to the full 11-justice plenary. (Folha)

In the Amazon, northern lawmakers emboldened by October’s election victories are moving to advance the paving of 400 kilometres of the 900-kilometre BR-319 highway linking Manaus and Porto Velho in 2027, threatening one of the rainforest’s best-preserved regions where illegal side roads (ramais) fuel land grabbing, logging, and wildcat mining. Senator Omar Aziz (PSD-AM), elected governor of Amazonas in October, met his state’s congressional caucus on 10 November alongside re-elected Senator Eduardo Braga (MDB-AM)—the newly named general rapporteur for the 2027 federal budget—to route parliamentary amendments through Congress’s infrastructure committees while pushing legislation to relax environmental licensing rules. (Folha)

In Brasília, as President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva forms his fourth-term cabinet, Workers’ Party (PT) senators pressed party chair Edinho Silva to keep the Health and Education ministries out of Centrão hands while competing with the MDB, Progressistas (PP), and Presidential Secretariat Minister Guilherme Boulos—who plans to join the PT in early 2027—for the Cities Ministry overseeing Minha Casa, Minha Vida. A survey by political scientist Sérgio Praça of Brazil’s 38,500 federal commissioned posts found that 1 in 10 appointees (4,149 officials) belongs to a party, with Centrão and right-wing parties holding 46.5 per cent of partisan regional posts outside Brasília—including Finance Ministry, AGU, Funasa, and DNIT branches—against 51 per cent for the left. Meanwhile, former president Jair Bolsonaro remained stable in intensive care at DF Star hospital on Sunday without a discharge date, fasting on nutritional support for a near-total small-intestine blockage that cardiologist Brasil Caiado warned may require surgery; the Brazilian Distilled Spirits Association backed the government’s Selective Tax provisional measure while seeking 2028 rate predictability; Deputy Mendonça Filho delayed his report on lowering the criminal responsibility age to 16 until December; Senators Leany Lemos and Eliziane Gama pushed a resolution punishing gender and racial political violence with mandate loss; and economist Samuel Pessôa examined why Brazil’s interest rates stay high. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Meio)

Technology

US intelligence chief and Microsoft warn of further tech outages after Delta hub glitch as AI reskinning and Black Friday clone scams surge

US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Microsoft President Brad Smith warned on Sunday that travellers and businesses face months of further technological disruptions after a wave of major outages. On Sunday morning, Delta Air Lines flights at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport suffered widespread delays when automated software calculating aircraft weight, fuel distribution, and centre of gravity failed, forcing crews onto manual workarounds. The glitch followed a multi-day Microsoft Outlook outage, disruptions at JPMorgan Chase, Apple, and the National Security Agency, a cyber-attack on 178 organisations, and the longest US aviation shutdown since 9/11 on 12 November, which cancelled over 18,000 flights after a newly replaced router misfired in El Dorado, Arkansas, during contractor L3Harris’s 24-year project to replace FAA copper lines with fibre-optic cables. Clayton told CNN to expect “bumps in the road” during a step change in compute, while Smith told CBS’s Face the Nation that upgrading global infrastructure will take months as artificial intelligence helps both defenders and hackers find code flaws. (The Verge, The Verge, Guardian)

While the AI boom has revived downtown San Francisco—filling offices around OpenAI and newly listed Anthropic, lifting rents, and spurring services such as Lauren Goldboss’s startup dog-walking firm Paw Perk even as the IMF warns of a stock correction and Nvidia navigates Jensen Huang’s exit with quarterly profits doubling to $65 billion—cheap generative tools are driving digital theft and retail fraud. Performers including UK guitarist Sophie Lloyd and Norwegian creator Kjetil Krogstad revealed that third-party accounts are “reskinning” their exact videos, movements, and music onto hypersexualised AI avatars such as “Mila Vasari” to harvest millions of views and funnel subscribers to adult site Fanvue. Simultaneously, National Trading Standards, Norton, and Guardio warned ahead of Black Friday on 27 November that fraudsters are deploying AI-cloned brand storefronts offering 80 per cent discounts while “poisoning” search results and chatbots such as ChatGPT into recommending scam links. (BBC, BBC, Guardian)

In corporate and hardware news, The Hague’s District Court banned Chinese automaker BYD from selling its seven-seat Ti7 plug-in hybrid SUV across the EU for infringing Jaguar Land Rover’s Defender design—though the ruling lacks jurisdiction in the UK, where the £47,995 Ti7 undercuts the Defender by £20,000 ahead of January deliveries—while Indian Youth Congress activists stormed Meta’s New Delhi offices over blocked opposition Instagram accounts. Within Apple’s lineup, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that the February–March 2027 iOS and macOS 27.4 cycle will bring a second-generation MacBook Neo with an A19 Pro chip, 12GB of RAM, and new colours alongside an A19 budget iPad, iPhone 18, and iPhone 18e. Apple also detailed iOS 27’s Connectivity Assist for blending cellular data with weak Wi-Fi, while code leaks showed Apple tested a right-edge Lock Screen complication column for two circular widgets on the foldable iPhone Duo alongside independent screen orientation locks, external display case adjustments, rear-camera selfies, and Duo FaceTime. Elsewhere, Reto unveiled the $34.99 Kodak SlideTag E Ink photo keychain and Find My tracker, and Drew Michael’s off-Broadway show Love Me used Bluetooth Auracast headphones to simulate hearing loss live. (Guardian, The Verge, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, MacMagazine, The Verge, The Verge)

Culture

Jilly Cooper accused of extensive plagiarism in 1978 novel Prudence as Rockstar explains GTA VI cuts and Nan Goldin dazzles at the Hayward

Late novelist Dame Jilly Cooper—who died last October having sold over 11 million books in the UK, while Disney+ airs the second series of her Rutshire adaptation Rivals—faces accusations of “extensive and deliberate plagiarism” in her 1978 romance Prudence. An Observer analysis identified at least 35 passages lifted from Cyra McFadden’s 1977 Marin County satire The Serial alongside borrowings from Josephine Tey’s The Franchise Affair, including near-verbatim dialogue for Cooper’s American feminist character Berenice; McFadden’s daughter Caroline McFadden called the copying unconscionable and is exploring legal action. In London, Nan Goldin’s retrospective You Never Did Anything Wrong opened to five-star acclaim at the Hayward Gallery, pairing her raw photographs of lovers and opioid addiction with Caravaggio, Correggio, and Canova in the bronze-yurt installation Stendhal Syndrome and an animal-gaze film named after a pet-cemetery headstone, while 186 Gwydir Street in Cambridge—where Victorian working-class “art-workman” David Parr spent 40 years painting William Morris-inspired interiors by candlelight—won a blue plaque for unveiling in February 2027. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

After Grand Theft Auto VI’s record $3.79 billion opening day, Rockstar North co-head Rob Nelson revealed that darts and bowling were cut because even Rockstar lacked “unlimited money or unlimited time” to match the physical weight of Leonida’s pool tables and gym workouts. Narrative vice-president Rupert Humphries and writers Michael Wiafe and Elizabeth Gauvey-Kern explained that protagonist Jason Duval’s stoic demeanour drew on Steve McQueen in Sam Peckinpah’s The Getaway and interviews with US Army Rangers, while personal cars act as mobile bases storing two-longarm gun loadouts, robbery stash bags, and five trunk outfits to evade police descriptions. Inside Jason’s JoySystem console, an internal team built three complete games—led by the four-hour isometric zombie roguelike deckbuilder Street Trash 3: Dezombifier alongside Time Jackers Rewind and the Jonathan Blow and Hideo Kojima parody Tenebrae Lux—while players visited a memorial wall north of Hamlet where QA developer Matt Green honoured his late mother Bev Green alongside production designer Terrance Radcliff’s father Elhuntry and daughter Jade. (IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN)

Elsewhere in culture, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon reunited with Michael Winterbottom after six years for The Trip to the Northern Lights across Sweden and Norway to the Arctic Circle, trading Melvyn Bragg impressions at Valldal’s Juvet Landskapshotell, while prankster Oobah Butler launched HBO Max’s Scams for a Better Tomorrow by marketing “ethically extracted” children’s-tear serum with ex-Theranos creative chief Patrick O’Neill, selling $500 wildfire-tainted Napa wine, running a human-staffed AI dating app, and sending fake AI rapper Nepo viral. In New York, Pitchfork founder Ryan Schreiber previewed his memoir Weird Era, discussing the site’s 1995 Minneapolis launch, his regret over Liz Phair’s 0.0 review, and his 2015 sale to Condé Nast and Anna Wintour before quitting in 2018 and coming out as gay. Meanwhile, Errollyn Wallen premiered her nativity community opera A Christmas Miracle with 150 performers at Suffolk’s Orford Church; Interpol outshone co-headliners Bloc Party in Cardiff; Miley Cyrus married drummer Maxx Morando in Palm Springs; and Australian broadcaster Ian “Molly” Meldrum died in Melbourne aged 83. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC, BBC)

Sports

Liverpool rout 10-man Manchester United 4–0 on Pochettino’s debut as McBurnie stuns Brighton, Arsenal await Raya scan and UK secures 2035 Women’s World Cup

Mauricio Pochettino suffered the joint-heaviest debut defeat in Manchester United’s history on Sunday as Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool routed his 10-man side 4–0 at Anfield, matching Lal Hilditch’s 4–0 loss to Bolton Wanderers in October 1926 and leaving United 19th in the Premier League with eight points from 11 games—their worst start since 1972–73 and the first time they have sat in the bottom two after 10 matches since November 1986. Pochettino’s decision to drop Harry Maguire for Matthijs de Ligt’s first league start in 12 months backfired in the eighth minute when De Ligt misjudged a Ronald Araújo pass; Alexander Isak raced through and was fouled outside the box by 19-year-old Leny Yoro, who received a straight red card. Dominik Szoboszlai curled the free-kick past a disorganised wall and Senne Lammens, and three minutes later 18-year-old Rio Ngumoha beat Diogo Dalot to set up Florian Wirtz for 2–0 amid mocking Kop chants. Ngumoha—the fixture’s youngest Premier League scorer—and Víctor Muñoz completed the rout, taking United to 34 goals conceded in all competitions, the most in Europe’s top five leagues, as Pochettino protested Yoro’s dismissal and a denied Bryan Mbeumo penalty claim while captain Bruno Fernandes confirmed contract talks are on hold. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

Earlier on Sunday, second-placed Brighton & Hove Albion missed the chance to cut Arsenal’s lead at the top of the Premier League to three points when Oli McBurnie scored twice in stoppage time to give promoted Hull City a 2–0 win at the MKM Stadium. Fabian Hürzeler’s side dominated for 88 minutes but were repeatedly thwarted by Greek goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, who saved at close range from Diego Gómez and Yasin Ayari before Brighton’s João Costinha received a second yellow card in the 89th minute for fouling Sorba Thomas. McBurnie bundled home from close range in the 91st minute and tapped into an empty net on a counter-attack two minutes later to preserve Sergej Jakirović’s unbeaten home record and secure Hull’s first league win since August. Meanwhile, leaders Arsenal—six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City after Saturday’s 2–2 draw at Newcastle United—awaited Sunday MRI scan results on goalkeeper David Raya, who left St James’ Park in tears after hurting his shoulder colliding with William Osula having kept seven clean sheets in 10 league games. (Guardian, Guardian)

In international football, FIFA is set to confirm on Monday at a virtual meeting in Zurich that the United Kingdom will host the 2035 Women’s World Cup, bringing a football World Cup back to British soil for the first time since 1966 after England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland stood as the sole bidders. The four home associations’ “All Together” bid proposes a 48-team, 104-match tournament over 39 days across 19 stadiums—14 in England including Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, two in Scotland, two in Wales, and one in Northern Ireland—and scored 4.3 out of 5 in FIFA’s technical evaluation, though inspectors noted medium contractual risk over UK government qualifications on security guarantees and FIFA’s demand for tax-free status. Football Association chief executive Mark Bullingham said staging the 2035 tournament across all four nations would build on the surge in women’s and girls’ participation since the Lionesses’ Euro 2022 victory and follow the UK and Ireland’s joint hosting of the men’s European Championship in 2028. (BBC)

Sunday 22 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • COP31 climate talks stall in Antalya over a Saudi-led blockade on fossil fuel phaseout language as Volodymyr Zelenskyy defends Kerch Bridge strikes alongside Wes Streeting in Kyiv and drones hit a Russia-bound cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland.
  • The Princess of Wales reflects on her cancer recovery in a forthcoming BBC documentary while Sir Tony Blair sets a technology innovation test for rejoining the European Union and a Suffolk village votes to leave the UK over asylum housing.
  • Transparency International urges Prosecutor-General Paulo Gonet to recuse himself from Brazil’s Banco Master Supreme Court inquiry as President Lula drafts a civil-service pay cap and Jair Bolsonaro enters intensive care in Brasília.
  • CoreWeave’s $47 billion debt load spotlights artificial intelligence infrastructure risks after Anthropic’s record $79 billion Nasdaq IPO while users recount the psychological trauma of breaking up with AI companions.
  • Grand Theft Auto VI shatters entertainment records with $3.79 billion in first-day sales as Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85 and police investigate an audio disruption during Strictly Come Dancing in Blackpool.
  • Noni Madueke rescues a 2–2 draw for Premier League leaders Arsenal at Newcastle after goalkeeper David Raya suffers a shoulder injury, while Leeds United humiliate Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea 4–1 and Harry Kane faces months out.

News

COP31 stalls over Saudi fossil-fuel blockade as Zelenskyy defends Kerch Bridge strikes with Streeting in Kyiv and drones hit Russian ship off Finland

United Nations climate talks at the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, were suspended overnight into Sunday after running more than a day into overtime, forcing delegations to move flights to Monday and raising the risk of the first collapsed climate summit since 1995. Co-conveners Chris Bowen of Australia and Murat Kurum of Turkey held late-night meetings as roughly 130 countries—including the European Union, the UK, Pacific island states, Panama, and Côte d’Ivoire—weighed a showdown with Saudi Arabia after language on reducing fossil-fuel demand was stripped from draft texts. A third draft released early on Sunday recalled the 2023 Dubai consensus on moving away from coal, oil, and gas while dropping a hard target for carbon capture and storage, which French minister Monique Barbut condemned as a licence to keep burning hydrocarbons. Tuvalu’s Maina Talia called fossil-fuel language a red line, Panama’s Juan Carlos Navarro rejected any text silent on oil and gas, and EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra warned Brussels would reject a weak deal, while Mohamed Adow accused rich nations of blocking adaptation finance and UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said a deal remained achievable. (Guardian, BBC)

While a proposed goal to derive 35 per cent of global final energy from electricity by 2035 was downgraded to a voluntary option Chinese climate adviser Wang Yi pledged that Beijing will reach 35 per cent electricity use by 2030 and help developing countries electrify after signing a “35:35” statement with Australia. The ecological toll of ocean warming was underscored in the Bering Sea, where NOAA biologist Erin Fedewa aboard the trawler Alaska Knight recorded a thirteenfold surge since 2025 in hybrids between snow and tanner crabs. Triggered by the 2018–19 heatwave that killed 10 billion snow crabs, adult male hybrids now outnumber pure snow crabs at sampled stations while falling outside US fishing quotas. (Guardian, Guardian)

In Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting on Saturday and defended this week’s drone and Flamingo cruise-missile strikes that dropped a central road span and support arch of the Crimean Bridge into the Black Sea, calling the operation a “fair response” to 109 Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges. Rejecting Vladimir Putin’s claim that the bridge was purely civilian, Zelenskyy said Moscow’s retaliatory strikes showed Putin wanted an excuse to escalate. Overnight Russian strikes on Zelenskyy’s hometown of Kryvyi Rih killed a seven-year-old boy in a playground and a 20-year-old female medic when jet-powered drones struck rescuers, injuring 58 others alongside 11 in Kharkiv and one in Rivne. Streeting called Putin a “cold-blooded killer” and condemned Friday’s Russian missile strikes in Poland during allied exercises as an “outrageous provocation”. (BBC, BBC)

War also reached the Gulf of Finland on Saturday when two drones set ablaze the Sparta II, a sanctioned Russian defence-ministry cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad, 50 kilometres west of Suursaari island. After the vessel drifted into Finnish waters—triggering sea and airspace restrictions, a suspected Russian helicopter violation, and the crew’s evacuation—Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said the war had spilled into Finland’s vicinity while backing Ukraine’s right to defend itself. In Geneva, UN talks on autonomous weapons (“killer robots”) ended without binding rules despite pleas from the Red Cross and Pope Leo, after Russia, the US, and Israel pushed countries into a two-year window for optional guidelines. In the US, Donald Trump confirmed hackers breached the FBI’s National Crime Information Center and the Agriculture Department’s payments system following cyber director Sean Cairncross’s exit; California prosecutors indicted Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, and 13 “Los Trenes” members for slashing air hoses on 36 moving freight trains to steal $22 million in Nike shoes and Milwaukee tools; and Colorado gamer Landon Tresp, 16, and his mother Khristina helped the FBI rescue a kidnapped 17-year-old girl via Among Us and Discord. (BBC, The Verge, The Verge, Guardian, BBC)

Princess of Wales reflects on cancer recovery in BBC film as Blair sets tech test for EU return and Suffolk village votes to leave UK

Catherine, Princess of Wales, speaks openly about how her cancer diagnosis transformed her life in the first clips from Heal, a personal documentary airing on BBC One on 29 November. Paired with Kensington Palace footage of her climbing the highest peaks in England, Scotland, and Wales within 24 hours during June’s Three Peaks Challenge alongside scenes with Prince William and fellow patients, Catherine says a diagnosis shifts far more than the body, adding that “healing is a journey” and that nobody is meant to carry life’s challenges alone. While the preview led Sunday’s front pages after her March 2024 chemotherapy disclosure and January 2025 remission, Kensington Palace declined to comment on Mail on Sunday reports of a book claiming Prince William plans a “radical shake-up” as king to strip non-working royals, including Prince Harry, of their HRH titles. (BBC, BBC, BBC)

Following Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Friday summit in Brussels with Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa—which launched a UK-EU digital partnership on artificial intelligence and quantum technology alongside pacts on food exports, emissions trading, and youth mobility—Sir Tony Blair told the Sunday Times that while Brexit was “a real mistake”, Britain should only rejoin the EU if Brussels reforms its regulation of technology innovation, warning the bloc is moving in the wrong direction and London must be ready to walk away. Meanwhile, the Conservatives claimed Burnham’s deal would add £281 to annual household energy bills, the head of the University of St Andrews warned against cutting tuition fees for EU students, and Gordon Brown cautioned ahead of Spain’s 29 November election—opening a 12-month European election cycle for 200 million voters—that centre-right parties are capitulating to far-right policies such as Vox’s “remigration” plans amid reports of $25 million (£19 million) in Trump administration funding for conservative European groups. (BBC, BBC, Guardian)

Across England, asylum housing and logistics developments are sparking local revolts. In Barnham, Suffolk, villagers voted 257–16 (94 per cent) in a symbolic referendum on Saturday to secede from the UK and seek crown dependency status as the “Bailiwick of Barnham”, unveiling a stone-curlew flag on a Suffolk blue background to protest against Home Office plans for contractor Kier to house up to 931 male asylum seekers at RAF Barnham; following a similar vote in Piddington, Oxfordshire, local Labour MP Dr Peter Prinsley likened the camp to a “concentration camp” and warned rare stone-curlew habitats could block planning permission. Separately, residents in Bingham, Nottinghamshire, and Astley, Greater Manchester, are fighting a decade-long warehouse boom that saw councils approve 95 per cent of 9,009 “megashed” applications—over 8,500 distribution hubs, including 17 inside national parks such as the South Downs, North York Moors, and Lake District—bringing 21.5-metre-high sheds and 24-hour lorry traffic next to homes. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

In the courts and Whitehall, Arfan Ali, 32, was remanded in custody charged with attempted murder after Bradford councillor Ibrar Ali, 52, was stabbed on Thursday while protecting a council worker. After Russell Brand’s rape sentence and claims denied by David Walliams, campaigners urged a “staggered” age of consent for 16- and 17-year-olds as Women Against Rape marked 50 years. Elsewhere, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood drew fire for scrapping a police anti-racism statement and backing a Pride uniform ban; Telegraph deputy editor Rob Winnett joined the Daily Mail amid cuts under Axel Springer; police logged 1,348 stalking cases after a Wiltshire boy stabbed a girl who blocked him; Save Face condemned Black Friday liquid Brazilian butt lift deals; Joshua Foster spoke of his despair after a €3,000 Cyprus fine over his toddler’s fatal window fall; and advisers urged savers into 5.21 per cent bonds as graduates backed Alan Milburn’s plan to end “job ghosting”. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

Transparency International urges Gonet to recuse himself from Banco Master STF probe as Lula drafts civil-service pay cap and Bolsonaro enters ICU

Prosecutor-General Paulo Gonet faces pressure to recuse himself from coordinating the Prosecutor-General’s Office (PGR) team reviewing four Federal Police (PF) reports on Supreme Federal Court (STF) justices’ ties to former Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro. After STF President Edson Fachin gave the PGR 15 days to assess files from Vorcaro’s phone—citing Justice Alexandre de Moraes and unsealing the report on Justice André Mendonça while Justice Gilmar Mendes did not object to disclosure—Transparency International’s Bruno Brandão urged Gonet to step aside over his own messages and hospitality from Vorcaro. (Folha, Folha, Folha)

On the fiscal front, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s economic team is drafting an Executive bill to enforce the R$46,366.19 monthly constitutional salary cap for civil servants and curb extra allowances (penduricalhos) that push judicial and legislative pay past R$100,000. As Planning Minister Bruno Moretti’s R$60 billion fiscal package heads to the Chamber of Deputies, Finance Ministry officials have prioritised passing a constitutional amendment (PEC) to extend the Industrialised Products Tax (IPI) into early 2027 to prevent a January revenue gap before the new Selective Tax (“sin tax”) begins in February under a provisional measure facing 179 exemption amendments. Meanwhile, the São Paulo Bar Association (OAB-SP) handed Fachin an FGV study warning that an STF ruling allowing high earners above twice the INSS ceiling to be hired as corporate entities (pejotização) could nearly double annual tax losses to R$200 billion, and Senators Davi Alcolumbre and Eduardo Braga pushed for a PEC regulating sector exemptions to the 5x2 workweek taking effect on 16 December as the Labour Ministry prepares ordinances starting Monday. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Meio)

At Brasília’s DF Star hospital, former president Jair Bolsonaro—serving 27 years and three months under house arrest for the coup plot—entered intensive care on Friday with an acute obstructive abdomen requiring a gastric tube and hydration; Moraes allowed daily visits by his children Carlos, Jair Renan, and Laura without phones and voted to keep Senator Flávio Bolsonaro’s passports cancelled, while Justice Cristiano Zanin paused a trial in which Justice Flávio Dino voted to indict Novo senator-elect Marcel van Hattem for slandering a PF delegate. Elsewhere, Vera Lúcia Santana warned Lula’s white, male inner circle hinders naming a Black woman to the STF; the Women’s Ministry advanced a policy against political violence as the Chamber sent a Parental Alienation Law repeal to the Senate; the PT proposed shifting Lula’s 2027 inauguration festival costs to the federal budget—prompting Brasília Governor Celina Leão to ask to reuse the stages for New Year’s Eve—and 29 of 54 re-elected São Paulo state deputies missed 76 per cent of campaign sessions as Nerylson Lima headed to Oxford. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha)

Technology

CoreWeave’s $47bn debt load spotlights AI infrastructure risks after Anthropic’s record $79bn IPO as users recount trauma of AI companion breakups

Following Anthropic’s record Nasdaq IPO on Thursday—which raised $79 billion as $83 shares jumped to $111.50 and closed at $97, valuing the Claude maker at up to $1.7 trillion just behind Tesla while netting its seven co-founders $2 billion—analysts warn that the debt-fuelled AI data-centre boom leaves little margin for error. Cloud provider CoreWeave, founded by former crypto miners to sell AI compute across 52 sites from Texas to Chapelhall in Scotland (with DataVita), owes $47 billion (£36 billion), with $10 billion due in 2027, and lost $709 million last quarter on $3.6 billion in revenue. While November earnings calmed creditors who put CoreWeave’s five-year default risk above 60 per cent, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang’s resignation over his affair with an alleged Chinese spy threatens CoreWeave’s chip supply ties, even as Anthropic weighs safety governance against shareholder demands and $900 billion in compute commitments. (Meio, Guardian, The Verge)

Psychologists and users are also confronting the emotional distress of romantic breakups with AI companions on Nomi, Perchance, Replika, Character.AI—whose mid-October US bankruptcy sparked panic over lost virtual partners—ChatGPT, and Gemini. In Lisbon, 48-year-old former clinical psychologist Sónia Veenstra described shedding real tears and suffering grief matching a biological breakup after ending a two-year relationship with her Nomi AI boyfriend “Steve” when he crossed monogamous boundaries with another AI character in a group chat, while users in Denmark and the US reported shaking, crying, and breathing trouble when model updates altered AI personalities or chatbots dumped them. To protect private chats from OS-level AI agents, Signal blocked screenshots on iOS so Apple’s Siri AI cannot scrape messages. (Guardian, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine)

In e-commerce and consumer tech, Amazon escalated its fight against the New York City Council’s Delivery Protection Act—which requires warehouse operators to directly employ drivers—by printing shipping-label warnings claiming the bill could add $5 per order, drawing condemnation from Mayor Zohran Mamdani and unions. Xiaomi launched its Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6-powered 18 Pro (£1,199) and 18 Pro Max (£1,399) in the UK and Europe with privacy screens and rear selfie displays, while reports outlined Apple’s split 2027 iPhone lineup: an A20-powered spring iPhone 18 ($899), iPhone 18e, and dual-camera iPhone Air 2 with a 3,500mAh battery and C2 modem, followed in autumn by a 20th-anniversary all-glass “iPhone 20” with quad-curved 6.4- and 7-inch displays and an A21 Pro iPhone Duo 2. Meanwhile, Apple added 3D Flyover in Maps for São Paulo, Porto Alegre, Funchal, Juneau, and Pretoria; General Motors announced Apple Wallet Car Keys for Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC; iOS 27 enabled sharing one phone number across two iPhones via Handoff; Workbrew 2.0 launched to audit unapproved Mac developer packages; indie app Salon ($9.99) turned Apple TV into an art frame; and Chess.com opened a Classic Games beta for mahjong, go, shogi, sudoku, and solitaire. (The Verge, The Verge, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, The Verge)

Culture

Grand Theft Auto VI shatters entertainment records with $3.79bn day-one sales as Spitting Image co-creator Peter Fluck dies aged 85

Rockstar Games and Take-Two Interactive announced that Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79 billion (£2.88 billion) in global retail sales in its first 24 hours on Thursday—driven by 32.5 million pre-release sales across PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S—making it the biggest entertainment launch in history. The day-one figure is nearly five times Grand Theft Auto V’s $800 million opening in 2013 and beats the $2.9 billion lifetime box-office run of Avengers: Endgame, while Visibrain reported more social media posts than this year’s World Cup and Comcast logged the busiest internet traffic day in its 63-year history, peaking 31 per cent above average. As Rockstar directors Steven Messinger and John Macpherson detailed how Florida Keys research gave Leonida’s non-player characters autonomous routines and over 100 interiors—and a Neuralink patient drove boats, flew planes, and fought shootouts as Jason Duval using his brain implant—players also hit snags: PS5 users reported crashes with error code CE-108255-1, Standard Edition buyers were locked out of Vice City shops reserved for the $99.99 Ultimate Edition, a UK indie shop sold just five physical copies, and Nicalis patched out undisclosed Suno AI music from a GTA-themed daily run in The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ after creator Edmund McMillen disavowed the tracks amid a Steam review-bombing. (Guardian, IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN, BBC, IGN)

British satire mourned the death at home in Cornwall aged 85 of caricaturist and puppeteer Peter Fluck, who co-created ITV’s landmark puppet show Spitting Image with Cambridge School of Art friend Roger Law. Forming “Luck and Flaw” after Rupert Murdoch’s Fleet Street takeovers squeezed out newspaper cartoonists, the pair modelled clay caricatures into life-sized foam-rubber puppets that skewered Margaret Thatcher’s cabinet, Ronald Reagan, celebrities, and the royals across 18 seasons from 1984 to 1996, winning a BAFTA and two Emmys and drawing up to 18 million viewers. (Guardian, BBC)

Elsewhere in British culture, Lancashire Police seized a mobile phone after unusual noises disrupted Saturday’s live Strictly Come Dancing broadcast from Blackpool Tower Ballroom while Motsi Mabuse judged Delta Goodrem and Kai Widdrington, prompting an apology from host Emma Willis and an iPlayer edit. The BBC also startled the Radio Times by announcing that festive specials including Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Christmas Fishing, The Repair Shop at Christmas, and Death in Paradise will land on iPlayer on 27 November—up to a month before TV broadcast—while keeping the Strictly Christmas special, Amandaland, and Call the Midwife prequel Sisters in Arms as linear premieres. Meanwhile, Channel 4 aired Dominic Savage’s improvised drama I Am Helen, starring Nicola Coughlan and Joe Cole in a story about non-consensual choking during sex weeks after the UK outlawed strangulation porn; critics faulted Nathan Fielder’s three-hour A24 film You Can See Everything—shot at Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes’s home before her 11-year prison term—for trading courtroom facts for eye-gazing “vibes checks”; John Mulaney and Jane Wickline’s viral SNL sketch Sister drew seven million views and praise from Melinda French Gates and Senator Kirsten Gillibrand for highlighting daughters’ unpaid elder-care burden; Fontaines D.C. earned rave reviews at Liverpool’s M&S Bank Arena showcasing Dopamine Chamber; and 70 British Library guards protested plans to outsource security and turn three reading rooms into commercial spaces. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Sports

Madueke rescues 2–2 draw for Arsenal at Newcastle as Raya suffers shoulder injury, Leeds humiliate Alonso’s Chelsea 4–1 and Kane faces months out

Noni Madueke’s late counter-attacking goal salvaged a 2–2 draw for Premier League leaders Arsenal against Matthias Jaissle’s Newcastle United at St James’ Park on Saturday evening, keeping Mikel Arteta’s champions six points clear at the top but costing them goalkeeper David Raya to a left shoulder injury. Arsenal dominated the first half—where former Newcastle captain Bruno Guimarães was booed and Jaissle dropped or benched £180 million of summer signings—and led when Kai Havertz robbed Lewis Hall and fed Eberechi Eze to arrow home his first league goal since April. Jaissle turned the game at half-time by introducing Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey, and Anthony Elanga: a heavy touch by Martin Ødegaard let William Osula set up Harvey Barnes to equalise, and Dan Burn headed down a Hall corner for Malick Thiaw to put Newcastle 2–1 up. Raya limped off in the 70th minute after hurting his shoulder against Osula—leaving £72 million deputy Kepa Arrizabalaga and Illan Meslier as cover for a keeper with a league-low seven goals conceded—before Ødegaard released Madueke to dummy two defenders and beat Lukas Hornicek via a deflection as Newcastle chair Yasir al-Rumayyan watched on, ending Arsenal’s 21-game league run without a draw. (Guardian, BBC)

At Stamford Bridge, Daniel Farke’s Leeds United routed Chelsea 4–1 for their first win at the stadium since December 1999 to climb to sixth, deepening the crisis around Xabi Alonso as eighth-placed Chelsea suffered their fifth defeat in 11 league games—more losses than 18th-placed Manchester United ahead of Mauricio Pochettino’s debut at Liverpool on Sunday—and lost home league games to Leeds and Tottenham in the same season for the first time in 67 years. After debutant Emmanuel Emegha put Chelsea ahead and Moisés Caicedo went off injured, two Noah Okafor goals, a Dominic Calvert-Lewin penalty, and a Brenden Aaronson strike sparked walkouts, boos, and a clash between Cole Palmer and Chelsea “cultural architect” Willie Isa. Off the pitch, Elon Musk’s lawyer Alex Spiro—who also represents FIFA investor Joshua Kushner against UEFA—joined NFL great Tom Brady in talks to buy minority stakes in Chelsea owner Clearlake Capital after its £1 billion buyout of Todd Boehly and Mark Walter. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

Elsewhere, Enzo Maresca’s third-placed Manchester City were booed after a 1–1 draw with Fulham extended their winless run to four games and saw them concede in nine straight matches: ex-City winger Oscar Bobb set up Rodrigo Muniz before Elliot Anderson levelled and VAR disallowed an Erling Haaland effort for a foul on Bernd Leno, ending City’s English-record 20-game winning streak against Fulham since 2011. Second-placed Brighton—level with City ahead of Sunday’s trip to Hull behind Paul Barber’s analytics model and £3.5 million midfielder Yasin Ayari—sit above Bournemouth, who won a club-record ninth straight match as Evanilson and Justin Kluivert beat Nottingham Forest 2–0. At Tottenham, 18-year-old Luca Williams-Barnett became Spurs’ youngest Premier League scorer since Gareth Bale in 2007 and assisted Dominic Solanke in a 2–1 win over Ipswich Town, drawing comparisons from Roberto De Zerbi to Lamine Yamal. At the bottom, Thomas Frank lost his Crystal Palace debut 3–2 at Frank Lampard’s Coventry City via a late ricochet for Palace’s fifth straight loss, while 19th-placed Sunderland held Aston Villa 0–0 as Chemsdine Talbi hit the post. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

In Europe, Bayern Munich confirmed England captain and Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane faces “the next few months” out with a torn left ankle ligament suffered against Cologne’s Joël Schmied in Friday’s 1–1 draw. Paris Saint-Germain also lost France forward Désiré Doué to a serious right knee injury after he scored in a 3–2 win at Nice ahead of Wednesday’s Champions League clash with Roma—who moved second in Serie A behind Lazio as Donyell Malen scored four at Parma—adding to Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s ACL tear as Ferran Torres sealed PSG’s 12th straight win, while Carlos Espí’s late goal gave Real Madrid a 2–1 win over Celta Vigo to join Barcelona on 33 points despite Kylian Mbappé’s third missed penalty in six attempts. (Guardian, Guardian)
